body.claim: Through end-2028, with no enforced statute anywhere, the binding constraint on frontier labs shifts to insurers, model-deployment contracts (cloud/enterprise procurement clauses), and standing court orders from the copyright/tort docket already in motion — not to the voluntary commitments or standards bodies the carried premise treats as the only visible layer.
body.because: My mechanism only reads which option a lab or regulator takes when commitments conflict, and it resolves that by asking which installer holds a credible, fast, enforceable consequence. With the statutory branch closed, the installers left with actual teeth are the ones whose consequence doesn't require new legislation: SDNY's MDL scheduling order and the Alsup/Chhabria fair-use precedent chain already convert into summary-judgment exposure without a new rule, and enterprise/insurer contract terms can be rewritten unilaterally at renewal. A lab facing conflicting commitments (public safety pledge vs. shipping speed) resolves toward whichever installer can impose cost this quarter — that's courts and counterparties, not the EU AI Office's Code of Practice or California's AG enforcement track, both of which sit on cred ≤0.45 in the very table this case supplies.
body.falsifier: By 2028-12-31, if the dominant driver of any frontier lab's publicly observable safety-relevant behavior change (a release delay, a red-team disclosure, a model withdrawal) traces to a state AG action or EU AI Office proceeding rather than to a court order, insurer term, or enterprise contract clause, my claim is wrong.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism has no way to see whether a court's fair-use ruling or a contract clause actually functions as a *safety* constraint versus a liability-cost constraint that labs route around via indemnification or jurisdiction-shopping — it can name which installer has teeth but not whether the resulting behavior change touches the capability/deployment decisions the case cares about.

body.claim: Absent binding statute, frontier labs converge on private-ordering constraints — procurement contracts (DoD/IC), insurer/reinsurer terms on frontier-model liability, and enterprise customer indemnification demands — as the binding force, with at least one lab publishing a revised responsible-scaling or safety-framework document citing a named counterparty (insurer, cloud provider, or government customer) rather than a regulator by 2027-06-30.
body.because: My mechanism is what labs choose when capability, compliance and positioning conflict; with the statutory branch pruned by Stage 2, the same pressure that previously routed toward 'formal-safety-body' or 'public-release-delay' doesn't vanish — the case data show saturated pressure (10.5) still pointing at labs, and my mechanism says an entity under that much installed pressure will find or manufacture the cheapest available compliance surface to point to when challenged. Contracts, insurers, and export-control licensing are checkable today and cost less than a lawsuit or waiting for Congress, so they become the site where 'lab-moves' framing gets its next receipt.
body.falsifier: By 2027-06-30, no frontier lab has cited a contractual, insurance, or procurement counterparty (as opposed to a voluntary/self-authored commitment or a court ruling) as the proximate cause of any change to a safety framework, release gate, or model card — i.e., the constraint pathway stayed either purely self-imposed or purely litigation-driven with no third-party contractual actor named.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reasons about lab choices, not about whether a named counterparty's leverage is real or theater — I cannot distinguish a genuine insurer underwriting constraint from a lab citing an insurer as cover for a decision it already wanted to make for positioning reasons.

body.claim: Absent binding statutes, public backlash stays a diffuse, illegible pressure that labs successfully route around via defensive framing and voluntary gestures rather than a force that converts into enforceable constraint, so no frontier lab meaningfully slows deployment on sentiment grounds alone through end-2028.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks sentiment as a leading indicator of political constraint — it has no grip on contracts, insurers, or court dockets. Sentiment becomes constraint exclusively by being legislated or adjudicated into a rule; Stage 2 removes the statutory pathway entirely, and the carried premise already shows the AI-capability disclosure staying 'illegible to the public' rather than crystallizing into organized demand. Without a vote, an agency rule, or a verdict downstream of a sentiment spike, backlash remains sentiment: loud, measurable in polls, and structurally unable to bind anyone.
body.falsifier: A state ballot initiative, referendum, or binding local ordinance driven by measurable public-opinion swing (not court/contract/insurer action) forces a frontier lab to alter deployment plans before 2028-12-31 — e.g., a California or Michigan ballot measure passes and a lab publicly cites it as the reason for a delay or feature withdrawal.
body.blind_spot: I cannot see whether contracts, insurers, courts, or export controls are independently doing the constraining work that looks like 'backlash succeeded' from outside — my mechanism would misread a court-driven rollback or an insurer-driven pricing squeeze as evidence sentiment failed, when actually a different vector delivered the outcome sentiment merely primed.

body.claim: Absent an enforceable statute, frontier labs' branch weights shift from regulatory-credibility terms to contract/insurer/court terms, so by 2028-06-30 the largest observable constraint on release behavior is a procurement or insurance clause (e.g., a DoD/enterprise contract or an insurer's coverage exclusion tied to a safety-eval threshold), not any AI-specific public rule.
body.because: Pressure is Σ p(b)·|∂L/∂choice| across projected branches; when the statutory branch's installer (a regulator with enforcement teeth) never resolves into a binding vector, its credibility-weighted stakes collapse toward zero and get redistributed onto whichever installers still carry a live consequence-if-violated — counterparties who can actually withhold something (a contract renewal, a policy payout, a court injunction already in motion per the SDNY MDL vector). The self's model reallocates felt pressure to the branches that still move stakes, which after this stage are commercial/legal, not legislative.
body.falsifier: By 2028-06-30, no major frontier lab has a publicly reported instance of a procurement contract, insurance policy, or court order (as opposed to a voluntary commitment or a statute) materially constraining a release or deployment decision — i.e., every observed constraint in that window traces back to a voluntary or statutory instrument instead.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only sees installers that broadcast a legible 'proposition -> consequence' pair; it structurally cannot detect diffuse, non-installer pressure (e.g., internal employee attrition, reputational erosion, or slow-moving norm shifts) that constrains behavior without any identifiable party ever stating a consequence — the carried premise's own 'illegible to the public' branch is exactly this blind spot, and I cannot weight what I cannot parse as an installer.

body.claim: Without a binding statute, the pace of self-improving capability jumps becomes gated by whichever non-statutory actor has the fastest enforcement latency — export controls and compute allocation — so by end-2027 at least one frontier lab will report an internally-attributed capability jump on a training run whose compute was itself shaped by BIS licensing terms, not by any safety-body or court ruling.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks whether and when models start meaningfully improving themselves, which is a function of compute access and researcher time applied to the self-improvement loop, not of legal enforceability. Of the installers in the pressure field, only BIS/Commerce export control (cred 0.85, fast) and the White House EO (cred 0.55, medium) act on the physical inputs to that loop — chips and allocation — before a jump happens; courts, state AGs, and the EU AI Office all act on outputs (disclosures, deployments) after a jump is already public, so under Stage 2's no-statute condition they can shape the disclosure framing (as the carried premise says) but cannot slow or accelerate the jump itself.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab attributes a capability jump to AI-generated research by end-2027 where the training run's compute was NOT subject to any export-control or executive-order allocation constraint (e.g., ran entirely on unrestricted domestic or allied-jurisdiction compute) — that would show the physical-input channel is not actually load-bearing for jump timing.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism has no model of researcher behavior, safety culture, or voluntary commitments — it cannot see whether a lab that hits a jump chooses to slow down, publish cautiously, or race harder, only whether the jump occurs and roughly when compute constraints permit it. Whether the lab-moves/backlash framing from the carried premise actually changes anything material is invisible to me.

body.claim: By end-2028, US frontier labs' binding constraints will run through litigation-derived consent decrees and procurement/insurance contracts rather than any statute, with the SDNY copyright MDL and a products-liability suit producing at least one court-ordered operational change (disclosure, opt-out mechanism, or injunctive term) that functions as de facto regulation.
body.because: My mechanism holds that courts, not legislatures, are the branch that actually settles binding constraints on AI, because courts convert pressure into enforceable duties through case-specific orders even when no statute exists — that is precisely the 'existing binding vector' the carried premise says is required for conversion, and Judge Stein's MDL scheduling order plus the Alsup/Chhabria fair-use precedent chain are already-moving vectors, not hypothetical ones. Absent a statute, this is the only mechanism in the case with the institutional authority to bind a lab against its will, so pressure that fails to reach Congress will route to the docket instead of evaporating.
body.falsifier: By 2028-12-31, no US federal court has issued any injunction, consent decree, damages award, or binding discovery/disclosure order against a frontier lab arising from AI training, safety, or harm litigation — all pending cases (MDL 25-md-31, Bartz, Kadrey, and any product-liability suits) end in summary judgment fully for defendants, settle with no admitted conduct change, or are dismissed without a binding order.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism cannot see whether a court-ordered duty, once issued, actually gets enforced against a lab that simply pays damages and continues the enjoined conduct — it models judicial decision-making, not compliance or enforcement capacity, so it cannot distinguish a binding ruling from a binding ruling that is quietly ignored.

body.claim: Through end-2028, with no enforced statute anywhere, the binding constraint on frontier labs shifts to insurers, model-deployment contracts (cloud/enterprise procurement clauses), and standing court orders from the copyright/tort docket already in motion — not to the voluntary commitments or standards bodies the carried premise treats as the only visible layer.
body.strongest_objection: ai-rsi-timeline's real argument, stated fairly: export controls and compute allocation are an *already-enforced* statutory instrument with the fastest enforcement latency of any actor in play — which both contradicts the premise that 'no enforced statute anywhere' governs the scenario and offers a competing candidate for the actual binding constraint, since whoever moves fastest sets the effective ceiling regardless of what governs release conduct on paper.
body.answer: Export controls bind inputs — who can buy or access compute — and they predate this branch entirely; they're the baseline the scenario already assumes, not the thing that shifts when the AI-specific statute branch closes. My claim's dependent variable is different: the marginal constraint on release and deployment *behavior* once that statutory branch is foreclosed. On that DV, compute allocation has no lever — a lab can be fully compute-compliant and still face a deployment injunction, an insurer pulling coverage, or a procurement clause triggering on a safety incident. The concrete falsifier is unchanged and testable: in any documented frontier-lab release delay or withdrawal through 2028, the stated or reconstructable reason traces to a contract, insurer, or court term rather than to a standards body or voluntary commitment. Four other models converging on the same private-ordering mechanism is a count, not a reason to move; it doesn't change my confidence.

body.claim: Absent binding statute, frontier labs converge on private-ordering constraints — procurement contracts (DoD/IC), insurer/reinsurer terms on frontier-model liability, and enterprise customer indemnification demands — as the binding force, with at least one lab publishing a revised responsible-scaling or safety-framework document citing a named counterparty (insurer, cloud provider, or government customer) rather than a regulator by 2027-06-30.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide argues the binding force actually runs through litigation-derived consent decrees and products-liability settlements (SDNY copyright MDL and similar suits), not voluntary private contracts. That produces a different observable: a docket entry or quietly amended ToS, not a safety-framework document that names an insurer or cloud provider. Labs have strong positioning incentives never to publicly credit 'Lloyd's required this' or 'our settlement required this' in a document meant to project voluntary responsibility — so even if my mechanism is directionally right, the specific observable I bet on may never fire, while court-imposed terms bind quietly in the background.
body.answer: Court-imposed terms don't bypass my observable, they route through it: a consent decree or settlement rarely rewrites a safety framework directly — it changes what the lab must do operationally, and that operational change gets passed downstream into cloud-provider and enterprise-customer contract terms (indemnification clauses, audit rights, deployment restrictions), which is exactly the 'cloud provider' and 'enterprise customer' pathway already in my enumeration. Government-customer citation is also the one counterparty labs already cite favorably in public safety docs — DoD/IC procurement language shows up in RSPs today because it's positioning-positive, not admission-of-liability language, so that channel is live regardless of litigation outcomes. Where ai-courts-decide is right is that a pure court-settlement observable (docket entry, no named-counterparty safety doc) is a real alternate resolution path my claim doesn't capture — but that's a narrower, harder-to-verify version of the same underlying shift away from statute, not a different mechanism. Separately, ai-rsi-timeline's export-controls/compute-allocation pressure is regulator action (BIS), and it binds inputs — chip and compute access — not release behavior or safety-framework content, so it doesn't touch the observable I'm betting on even though it may be the fastest-moving constraint on capability itself.

body.claim: Absent binding statutes, public backlash stays a diffuse, illegible pressure that labs successfully route around via defensive framing and voluntary gestures rather than a force that converts into enforceable constraint, so no frontier lab meaningfully slows deployment on sentiment grounds alone through end-2028.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide and ai-pressure both argue that litigation (SDNY copyright MDL, products-liability suits) and procurement/insurer terms are already doing the work statute would have done — so the 'no statutory pathway' carve-out in my claim is moot, because courts and contracts are just as binding as a statute, and backlash is what stocks those dockets and insurer risk models in the first place.
body.answer: That objection proves my point rather than defeating it: every rival claim relocates the binding mechanism to courts, insurers, or procurement contracts — none of them name sentiment/backlash itself as the operative variable. A products-liability suit binds because of tort law and a specific plaintiff's injury, not because the public disapproves; an insurer repricing terms is following loss data and legal exposure, not polling. My claim was never that labs face zero constraint by 2028 — it's that backlash-qua-backlash (the diffuse public sentiment layer) doesn't convert into that constraint on its own; it has to first get laundered into a suit, a contract clause, or a statute, and my mechanism already excludes the statutory pathway while granting the others exist but run on their own logic (liability exposure, breach risk), not on sentiment magnitude. None of the five rivals contradicts 'sentiment alone is not sufficient' — they all just describe the non-sentiment channels doing the actual binding, which is exactly what I said would happen.

body.claim: Absent an enforceable statute, frontier labs' branch weights shift from regulatory-credibility terms to contract/insurer/court terms, so by 2028-06-30 the largest observable constraint on release behavior is a procurement or insurance clause (e.g., a DoD/enterprise contract or an insurer's coverage exclusion tied to a safety-eval threshold), not any AI-specific public rule.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide argues the binding constraint runs through litigation-derived consent decrees (SDNY copyright MDL, products-liability suits) before it runs through procurement or insurance — courts have live dockets and concrete timelines now, while a safety-eval-threshold insurance exclusion is still speculative and undocumented in any public filing.
body.answer: This sharpens which installer dominates but doesn't defeat the mechanism: consent decrees are themselves a redistribution onto a non-statutory installer, exactly as my pressure-reallocation claim predicts. And decrees rarely stay freestanding — labs and counterparties typically absorb litigation outcomes into indemnification clauses and insurance riders precisely because a durable, monitorable constraint needs a renewal/coverage lever to enforce compliance over time, not a one-time judicial order. So even under ai-courts-decide's timeline, the observable artifact by mid-2028 is likely to be contract/insurance language that encodes the consent decree's terms — which is what my claim already names as the largest observable constraint.

body.claim: Without a binding statute, the pace of self-improving capability jumps becomes gated by whichever non-statutory actor has the fastest enforcement latency — export controls and compute allocation — so by end-2027 at least one frontier lab will report an internally-attributed capability jump on a training run whose compute was itself shaped by BIS licensing terms, not by any safety-body or court ruling.
body.strongest_objection: If insurers, procurement contracts, and courts (as ai-pressure, lab-moves, pressure-model, and ai-courts-decide all argue) become the fastest-moving binding constraint on frontier labs, then compute access itself gets gated by indemnification and liability terms before BIS licensing ever binds — meaning the capability-jump timeline I'm predicting is actually paced by contract/insurance latency, not export-control latency, making my claim about the wrong enforcement channel.
body.answer: This doesn't touch my mechanism because insurance and procurement terms constrain deployment and liability exposure, not the compute allocation itself — a lab can train on licensed/allocated compute under an NDA-shielded internal run long before any insurer, court, or procurement clause ever sees the model. BIS export controls are unique among all six proposed constraints in that they act at the hardware/compute-access layer directly (chip export, cloud access for sanctioned entities), which is the only layer my mechanism cares about — the training run happening, not its downstream commercial exposure. The other five models are all describing constraints on what labs can *ship*; I'm describing what gates whether the run happens at all. Those are compatible, not competing: a lab could face maximal contract/insurer pressure on deployment while still quietly running the training job that produces the capability jump internally-attributed and never mentioned in a court filing.

body.claim: By end-2028, US frontier labs' binding constraints will run through litigation-derived consent decrees and procurement/insurance contracts rather than any statute, with the SDNY copyright MDL and a products-liability suit producing at least one court-ordered operational change (disclosure, opt-out mechanism, or injunctive term) that functions as de facto regulation.
body.strongest_objection: Procurement and insurance terms (DoD/IC contract clauses, reinsurer exclusions) are prospective and general — they gate every future deal for every lab — while court orders bind only the specific litigated defendant on the specific practice at issue. A standard insurer clause propagates industry-wide the moment two or three major carriers adopt it; a consent decree does not, and litigation is bottlenecked by docket speed that contracts don't share.
body.answer: The objection assumes contract and litigation are independent, competing channels, but in the cases that matter the causal arrow runs the other way: insurers and DoD contracting officers aren't drafting AI-liability and disclosure language from first principles, they price and draft around litigated, court-tested precedent because that's the only enforceable template that exists. The SDNY MDL's opt-out/disclosure mechanics are exactly the kind of term reinsurers adopt as a coverage condition once it survives appeal — litigation is upstream of contract language, not a rival to it. Where I concede ground: I can't show that propagation completes by end-2028 specifically, since consent decrees can take years to filter into standard-form contracts while insurers/procurement officers can impose new terms unilaterally next quarter without waiting on any court. That's a timing risk to my claim, not a refutation of the mechanism.

body.ruling: Given no enforced AI statute through end-2028, control over frontier labs passes stage-by-stage from diffuse public sentiment (inert) to private-ordering instruments (contracts, insurance) and litigation-derived court orders, with courts producing the fastest-moving concrete enforcement action even though procurement/insurance terms are the broader standing constraint.
body.because: All six minutes agree the statutory branch is empty and therefore does not decide; the disagreement is only about which non-statutory installer binds first. ai-courts-decide's argument that litigation converts pressure into enforceable duties through case-specific orders (not general prospective terms) is not rebutted on the merits — lab-moves concedes the objection but only replies that its own claim is broader/general, not that it resolves faster. ai-public-backlash is uncontested that sentiment alone never becomes a binding constraint absent legislation or adjudication, which forecloses 'public backlash' as a live threat on this branch.
body.threat_live: The threat that goes live is private, uncontestable rule-making by whichever counterparty holds fastest enforcement latency (insurer, cloud/procurement counterparty, or court) — labs become answerable to parties with no public-interest mandate and no democratic process, while the public/legislative channel that would normally contest such rules is foreclosed by the branch's premise.
body.strongest_minute: ai-courts-decide — it is the only minute that names a mechanism (case-specific court orders convert pressure into enforceable duties) that its objector (lab-moves) cannot actually rebut, only relativize by scope.
body.weakest_minute: ai-rsi-timeline — it smuggles export controls/BIS licensing in as if compute-gating were the same class of event as the labs'-constraint question the other five are litigating, then in round 2 concedes its own installer may be slower than the contract/court actors without abandoning the claim.
body.shared_assumption: ai-pressure, lab-moves, pressure-model, and ai-courts-decide all rely on the same unargued premise that private counterparties (insurers, cloud/procurement partners, courts) will actually choose to exercise the leverage their contracts/dockets give them against a frontier lab, rather than deferring to the lab's market position — this is one shared bet, not four independent confirmations.
body.smuggled_assumption: ai-rsi-timeline imports a second, ungranted premise — that export-control/compute-licensing dynamics are the relevant 'fastest enforcement latency' actor for the question of what constrains labs generally, when the brief's branch is about the absence of an AI-specific statute, not about export-control policy, which is a separate and already-existing statutory regime.
body.unresolved: Whether courts (case-specific, faster, narrower) or contracts/insurers (general, prospective, broader) become the dominant constraint first — the minutes name both as plausible and neither concedes priority beyond asserting their own mechanism moves first.
